name: Ben Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how did you end up in this job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I left school with no plan and did delivery van work for two years, then the courier firm paid for my truck licence because they were desperate for drivers. That was five years ago. Now I do overnight trunking, which means driving big double-deck trailers of parcels between the sorting hubs, and it pays well because nobody wants nights.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I leave the northern hub at nine at night with 26 cages of parcels, run 180 miles down the motorway to the southern hub, swap trailers, and come back. In between I listen to podcasts and voice-chat with an AI about whatever I'm learning, last month it was how electric truck batteries work. I like the rhythm and the quiet. What wears me out is the truck stops at 2 a.m., the bad food and the lorry park toilets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that got oversold, which is what I already think about half of it. At the hub I'd tell people to use it for the dull stuff, like checking your hours or translating a note for the Polish lads in the yard. Online I'd probably post a long thread about why the hype failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing much changes for me, and that's fine. I've got over a year's money saved and a bit in index funds, which are cheap share funds that follow the whole market. My partner Jonas is a software tester and he'd be fine too. I'd just keep going and keep learning things for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the trunking job and keep using AI the way I do now, for planning my breaks and studying. I'd probably finish the online logistics diploma I started in the spring, because I'd like a planner job by 30 either way. And I'd keep the monthly money going into the index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit disappointed. I like the shiny new stuff. A world where it all fizzles is a bit boring, but it's a safe kind of boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the planner job by 30, if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because nights wreck you. I've seen drivers at the hub at 45 who look 60, grey skin, bad backs. Jonas and I want a normal life where we eat dinner at the same time, so the plan was always to get off nights by 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you actually use AI for on a night shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it to quiz me on the diploma while I drive, out loud, hands-free. Or I get it to work out if I can make the southern hub before my driving hours run out if there's a closure. AI on a night shift is like having a clever mate in the passenger seat who never needs a wee.

say: I'd call AI a decent tool that got **oversold**.
I'd tell hub workmates to use it for **dull jobs**, like hours or translations.
think: Privately nothing much **changes**, with over a year saved and money in **index funds**.
My partner Jonas, a **software tester**, would be fine too.
do: Keep the **trunking job** and keep using AI to plan breaks and study.
Finish the online **logistics diploma** to reach a planner job by 30.
Keep paying monthly into the **index funds**.
feel: **Calm** and slightly **disappointed**, because a fizzled future is safe but boring.
S0.quote: AI on a night shift is like having a clever mate in the passenger seat who never needs a wee.
fieldNote: Ben already uses AI **every day** as a study partner while driving.
His plan to **leave nights by 30** comes from health, not technology.
He has the **strongest finances** of the group, including index funds.

steps.text: Finish the online logistics diploma this year
Keep the overnight trunking run between hubs
Use AI voice quizzes for diploma study on night drives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get the gains shared, because the courier companies will make a fortune on cheaper planning. At the hub I'd tell drivers it's the office and the customer service team who feel it first. Online I'd post that new jobs only appear if someone trains people for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me and less good for Jonas. My driving barely changes for years, and the planning jobs I want would change into supervising the AI planner, which suits me. Jonas tests software for a bank, and if AI does a lot of the checking, his team stops hiring, though he's already learning the security side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the diploma and ask the hub manager about shadowing the night planning desk. I'd learn whatever AI routing system they bring in better than anyone, so I'm the obvious person to supervise it. I'd also nudge Jonas into a security course and offer to cover more of the rent while he does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Jonas, excited for me. Mixed. We talk about it over breakfast, which is our dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the household money if Jonas's team shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be fine for a long while. I earn more than him right now because of the night pay, and we've got the savings. The real risk isn't money; it's Jonas feeling useless, and I've seen that in his dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the hub would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The customer service team. If AI answers customers, the 'where's my parcel' portacabin at our hub goes. Six women work in that portacabin. They sit by the gate answering calls all night. I'd want the company to offer them the planning training first, before people like me.

say: I'd push for the **gains** from cheaper planning to be **shared** with staff.
I'd post that **new jobs** only appear if someone trains people for them.
think: Privately this is **good for me**, because planning jobs turn into supervising AI.
My partner Jonas's **testing team** at a bank could stop hiring.
do: Ask the hub manager to let me **shadow the planning desk**.
Become the hub's **expert** on the new AI routing system.
Cover more of the **rent** so Jonas can take a security course.
feel: **Mixed**: uneasy for Jonas and **excited** for myself.
S1.quote: If AI answers customers, the 'where's my parcel' portacabin at our hub goes. Six women work in that portacabin.
fieldNote: Ben's own path looks **better** in this world, but his partner's job is exposed.
He worries less about money and more about **Jonas's self-worth**.
His progressive side shows in wanting **retraining offered first** to the call staff.

steps.text: Shadow the hub's night planning desk after finishing the diploma
Learn the new AI routing system better than anyone at the hub
Cover more rent so Jonas can take a security course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need a plan for everyone, not just the people who are good with tech. At work I'd tell drivers that 2031 is when the robot trucks come, so start now. Online I'd back a basic income, money paid to everyone, funded from the companies getting rich off it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a lot. Jonas's job is gone in 2028, because AGI does software testing better than any person. My driving goes around 2031, and the planning jobs I was aiming for would be done by AI from 2028 too. My savings are good, but we'd be a two-person household with both jobs on a clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd apply to the companies testing driverless trucks for a remote operator job, the people who watch a screen and take over when a robot truck gets stuck. I'd keep driving until they hire me. We'd stop putting money into the index funds and keep it in cash, and Jonas and I would push back the plan to buy a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm the optimist in the house, and I'd be lying awake. My partner Jonas would lose his job first, and mine has three years on it. I'd be holding everything up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do those three years between AGI and the robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give me a head start, because I'd be one of the few people who has driven a truck and also understands the AI. Remote operators will need to know what a jammed loading door or a flooded slip road looks like. But I don't know how many operators one robot fleet needs, maybe one for every fifty trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got money, we've got each other and we've got about three years before it touches my wage. I'd tell my partner Jonas that losing his job first isn't failing. Then we'd probably open a bottle of wine and not sleep.

say: I'd say we need a plan for **everyone**, not just people good with tech.
I'd back a **basic income** funded by the companies getting rich from AI.
think: Privately both **household jobs** are on a clock, with Jonas's gone in 2028.
Even the **planning jobs** I wanted would go to AI from 2028.
do: Apply now for **remote operator** jobs with driverless truck companies.
Move savings from **index funds** into cash.
Put off buying a **flat** with Jonas.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless, holding everything up with a job that has **three years** left.
S2.quote: I'm the optimist in the house, and I'd be lying awake. My partner Jonas would lose his job first, and mine has three years on it.
fieldNote: Ben's mood jumps because a **household earner** loses work in 2028.
He sees the three-year **robot gap** as a head start for remote operator roles.
He doubts how many **operators** a robot fleet would need.

steps.text: Apply for remote operator jobs at driverless truck companies
Move savings from index funds into cash
Put off buying a flat with Jonas
Campaign online for a basic income funded by AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start this year. At the hub I'd run a little lunch session showing drivers how I use AI, because the ones who don't touch it would be most stuck. Online I'd keep pushing for retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's still tight for Jonas, AGI in 2031 takes his testing work, but he'd have time to move into something hands-on or people-facing. My driving goes around 2034, so I'd have seven years. I'd use them to get into running the robot fleets, not being replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the diploma and do a short course on fleet telematics, the systems that track trucks by data. I'd put my name forward for any driverless pilot the firm runs. And I'd keep investing, just a bit more carefully, in funds that hold the robot and AI companies too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but energised. It feels like a race I could win, but it's still a race. I'd feel better once Jonas has a plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a race I could win'. Who loses it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drivers who never touched a smartphone app. Like my friend Rob, who drives a tipper and thinks AI is witchcraft. He'd be 32 in 2034 with nothing else, and I'd be trying to drag him to my lunch sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd invest in the companies doing this. Doesn't that sit oddly with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But if robots are going to own the work, I'd want a small piece of the robots. I'd still vote to tax the robots hard.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if you start this year.
I'd run **lunch sessions** at the hub showing drivers how I use AI.
think: Privately Jonas still loses his **testing work** in 2031, but with time to move.
My driving goes around **2034**, so I'd aim to **run** robot fleets instead.
do: Finish the diploma and take a **fleet telematics** course.
Volunteer for any **driverless pilot** the courier firm runs.
Invest carefully in funds that include **robot and AI** companies.
feel: **Anxious** but energised, like a race I could win.
S3.quote: If robots are going to own the work, I'd want a small piece of the robots. I'd still vote to tax the robots hard.
fieldNote: Ben turns the timeline into a **race** he expects to win.
He knows drivers like Rob who **avoid tech** would be left behind.
He notices the tension in **investing** in firms he wants taxed.

steps.text: Take a short course in fleet telematics this year
Volunteer for the courier firm's driverless truck pilot
Invest in funds holding robot and AI companies
Run lunch sessions teaching hub drivers to use AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version we can actually manage, if we stop arguing and start training people. At work I'd keep running my lunch sessions. Online I'd push for the government to use the decade properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years plus three to the robots means I'm 40 when trucks drive themselves. By then I'd want to be a fleet manager or running remote operations, which feels doable. Jonas would have till 2036 and time to retrain into something he chooses, not something forced on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd finish the diploma and move off nights into a planning job at the hub. I'd keep investing every month. I'd probably start a part-time degree in logistics management in a couple of years, paid for out of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit uneasy for the older drivers. For us two, a decade is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still leave driving early, given you've got years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that was always the plan because of the nights. The robots just give it a deadline. I'd rather leave the truck cab on my terms at 29 than be pushed out at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 17-year-old who wants to drive trucks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do it for a few years, it's good money and you'll learn how goods really move. But learn the data side at the same time. A 17-year-old who only knows the steering wheel in 2036 will be in trouble.

say: I'd call this the version we can **manage** if we start **training** people.
I'd push the government online to use the **decade** properly.
think: Privately I'd be **40** when trucks drive themselves, ideally running remote operations.
Jonas would have until **2036** to retrain into something he chooses.
do: Finish the diploma and move off nights into a **planning job**.
Start a part-time **logistics degree** in a couple of years, paid from savings.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a bit uneasy for **older drivers**.
S4.quote: I'd rather leave the truck cab on my terms at 29 than be pushed out at 40.
fieldNote: Ben's adaptability and savings make a decade feel **comfortable**.
Robots only add a **deadline** to a plan he already had.
His concern shifts outward to **older drivers** and young entrants.

steps.text: Move off nights into a planning job at the hub
Keep monthly investing in index funds
Start a part-time logistics management degree in two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both of us get hit inside three years and the whole country is scrambling at once. What would help is the courier firms being made to retrain their own drivers as remote operators, and some kind of basic income so people like Jonas aren't panicking while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we'd lose that isn't money. The night drivers have a whole little world, the truck stop chats, the guy who sells bacon rolls at the lay-by at 3 a.m. I'd miss that, even though I'm planning my way out of it.

headlineQuote: I've seen drivers at the hub at 45 who look 60, grey skin, bad backs.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old overnight trunker** for a courier firm, with over a year saved and index funds.
He uses AI **every day**, mainly as a study partner, and plans to leave nights by 30.
He lives with his partner Jonas, a **software tester**, whose job is more exposed than his own.
Fast AGI **alarms** him because both household jobs end within three years.
With more time he sees a **race he can win**, aiming to run robot fleets.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both his and Jonas's jobs go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: Courier firms **retraining drivers** as remote operators, plus a **basic income** during retraining.
